Welcome
Welcome to Big Deer State Park. The park is in the Groton State Forest Recreation Area and is close to the Groton Nature Center, Boulder Beach State Park and Stillwater State Park.
As early as 1704, Native Americans and French travelers used routes through Groton to reach Canada and Massachusetts. Settlers came to this part of Vermont earlier than other areas because the waterways made travel easier.
In the past, the hills were covered with trees such as white pine, spruce, hemlock, beech, maple, and birch. Local farmers cut these trees for lumber, fuel, and potash. Logging was a major industry in the area for nearly 100 years while the railroad was in use.
Today, logging is still important, but the area is also used for recreation. Many people visit for outdoor activities or stay in seasonal homes and cottages.
Groton State Forest covers more than 26,000 acres. It is the second largest area managed by the Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation. The forest includes more than 17 miles of hiking trails and over 20 miles of gravel roads and multi-use trails for mountain biking and horseback riding.
Facilities and Amenities
The park has 22 tent and RV campsites and 5 lean-to shelters. Firewood is available.
There is a restroom with flush toilets, hot and cold running water, and hot showers that use tokens. You can get shower tokens at the contact station during regular hours.
Big Deer State Park is close to the six other parks in Groton State Forest. While it is mainly a campground, you can also visit nearby parks for more activities and attractions.
Park Interpreter
This park has a park interpreter offering fun, hands-on activities in the new nearby Groton Nature Center. Interpreters are staff who help visitors learn about the park’s natural and cultural history. Programs may include night hikes, nature crafts, games, campfire programs, and amphibian exploration.
Check out the event calendar to see some of the programs planned during your visit.

Welcome
Image
The recently renovated Rocky Point House now serves as a museum and function area
Kill Kare State Park sits on the southwestern tip of St. Albans Point, a three-mile peninsula that forms St. Albans Bay. The park is surrounded on three sides by Lake Champlain.
The park is named after Kill Kare Camp, a summer camp for boys that operated here from 1912 to 1966.
At the center of the park stands a three-story building called Rocky Point House. Built in the 1870s, it first served as a summer resort hotel known as The Rocky Point House. The hotel operated under several owners until 1912, when the boys’ camp purchased the property.
From Camp to State Park
In 1967, the State of Vermont purchased the 17-acre property after the camp closed. The state needed a mainland location to support Burton Island State Park, which is accessible only by boat.
After the purchase, the cottages were removed and a public boat launch was built on the east shore. A breakwater was also added to protect the boat launch and ferry dock.
At first, the park mainly supported travel to Burton Island. Some group picnicking was allowed, but most activity was related to the island.
By the mid-1970s, more visitors began coming to swim and picnic. During this time, water quality in St. Albans Bay was poor in some areas, but visitors appreciated the relatively clean water and cool lake breezes at Kill Kare.
Restoring Rocky Point House
In the early 1980s, the park became more popular and needed updates. Rocky Point House was renovated in 1982, but by 2009 the building required more extensive work.
In 2010, the State of Vermont completed a major renovation. The project restored the building so it would reflect the lakeside hotel style of the late 1800s. The work was a partnership between the Vermont Division for Historic Preservation and the Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation.
Today, Rocky Point House is recognized as an important historic building for both the St. Albans community and the state of Vermont.
Museum
Rocky Point House now serves as a museum, dedicated in August 2012. Exhibits share the history of the site, including the hotel years, the boys’ camp, and the development of the state park.
Facilities and Amenities
Image
The Rocky Point House lawn, with pavilion visible in the background
Kill Kare State Park has a south-facing swimming area and a public boat launch. Visitors can also rent boats through the park. Potable water is available only inside the Rocky Point House. There are no water fountains in this park.
Island Runner Ferry
The Island Runner is a passenger ferry that runs between Kill Kare State Park and Burton Island State Park. It carries people and bikes (no vehicles or boats) back and forth several times a day. If you don't have your own boat, this is the only way to get to Burton Island.
The ferry operates from 7 days a week from Memorial Day Weekend through Labor Day Weekend and is piloted by a licensed captain and friendly crew. The ferry ride between Kill Kare and Burton Island is about ten minutes.
If you just want to spend a few hours on Burton Island, a ferry ride makes for a fun day excursion. If you are camping on Burton Island and you don't have your own boat, this is the only way to get you and your gear over to the island. Once on Burton Island, you can either use the carts provided to get your gear to your site, or you can choose to pay for gear delivery.
Island Runner Ferry schedule and fares (PDF)
Group Rentals
Image
The pavilion can be rented separately or in conjunction with the Rocky Point House function room, porch and lawn area
Kill Kare State Park offers several spaces for group events.
The West Function Room in Rocky Point House seats up to 22 people and works well for small meetings or wedding receptions.
The park also has a 26-by-40-foot open-air pavilion. The pavilion is universally accessible and includes electricity and a large cooking grill. It can be reserved for group functions.
For larger gatherings, the function room, the surrounding southeast lawn, and the pavilion can be rented together. These combined spaces can accommodate up to 300 people and are often used for weddings, receptions, and other large events.

Welcome
Image

As early as 1704, Native Americans and the French traveled through Groton on routes to Canada and Massachusetts. Colonists settled this part of Vermont slightly earlier than other areas because the waterways made it more accessible.
The hillsides were originally covered with white pine, spruce, hemlock, beech, maple, and birch. Local farmers logged the area for lumber, fuel, and potash. Logging grew into a large-scale industry for nearly 100 years while the railroad operated. Today, logging is still important but less dominant, as the area now also supports recreation, seasonal homes, private cottages, and park development.
Facilities and Amenities
The campground sits on the shores of Kettle Pond, an undeveloped pond. It has:
26 lean-tos arranged in five groups.
3 composting toilets and 2 double pit toilets.
No potable water on site. Water is available at nearby New Discovery State Park.
A campers’ beach.
Miles of hiking and multi-use trails throughout Groton State Forest.
7 remote lean-tos and 1 remote campsite for those seeking more seclusion.
The Groton Nature Center, nearby, serves all seven parks in the forest with educational programs and information.
Day Use Parking
Day-use parking for hiking and boating is separate from the campground, located along VT Route 232. The hiking trail and boat portage trail start at the northwest corner of the parking area near the kiosk.

Welcome
In the early 1800s, settlers cleared fields, rocks, and stumps in Ricker Basin and Cotton Brook. A settlement of about 50 families once lived in this area. Farming was difficult, and harsh weather made life challenging. Over time, younger generations left the area. Today, old cemeteries, sawmill remains, historic town roads, bridges, and many cellar holes can still be seen as evidence of a past community.
On November 3 and 4, 1927, torrential rains caused local rivers to rise and drove residents to their roofs. Between 1935 and 1938, the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), working with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, constructed Waterbury Reservoir. The CCC camp here was a large and active community with more than 80 buildings, housing about 2,000 men at its peak. Today, only a few chimneys and concrete foundations remain.
Today, Little River State Park is one of the most popular parks in central Vermont. Waterbury Reservoir is particularly popular for boating, with some areas set aside for quieter recreation. Angling for bass and trout is just as popular as water-skiing.
Enjoy swimming beaches, play areas, boat rentals, a boat launch, and miles of hiking and mountain bike trails in the adjacent Mt. Mansfield State Forest. Self-guided nature and history trails begin close to the camping area.
Facilities / Amenities
Image
The Bobcat cabin at Little River
Little River State Park, which is part of Mt. Mansfield State Forest, is home to central Vermont's largest and most popular campground. The campground has 81 tent and RV campsites, 20 lean-tos, and five cabins. Restrooms have flush toilets and hot and cold running water, and three of the four restrooms also have token-operated hot showers. A sanitary dump station is available, but there are no hookups.
Within the campground, there are swimming beaches, play areas, a boat launch, ball fields, and boat rentals for campers (for day-use boat rentals and swimming, see Waterbury Center State Park). Nearby are miles of hiking trails for campers and day-use visitors that highlight the rich cultural and natural history of the area.
Remote camping
The remote campsites can be reserved online or through the Reservation Call Center at 1-888-409-7579. Sites that are not reserved are available on a first-come, first-served basis. Information about open campsites may be found at each access area. If you find an open designated campsite, you may set up camp and a park ranger will stop by to register you.
Every remote campsite has a maximum occupancy of six people, unless otherwise posted. There are privies at these sites, but there is no drinking water available. View the remote camping page for more information.
Park Interpreter
Image
Staff lead a nature hike as part of the nature programs at Little River State Park
This park has a park interpreter offering fun, hands-on activities. A park interpreter is a staff member who helps visitors learn about the park’s natural and cultural history.
Some popular activities include night hikes, nature crafts and games, campfire programs, and amphibian explorations.
Check out the events calendar to see some of the programs planned during your visit.

This park is one of seven parks in the Groton State Forest. These parks are all within close proximity to one another. Some are within walking distance! Entry to one provides free entry to all. Combined, the parks offer a range of activities and attractions.
Welcome
Image
The trail leading up Owl's Head
Welcome to New Discovery State Park. As early as 1704, Native Americans and French travelers used routes through Groton to travel between Canada and Massachusetts. Later, colonists settled this area earlier than many other parts of Vermont because waterways made travel and transportation easier.
The rocky, tree-covered hillsides were once filled with white pine, spruce, hemlock, beech, maple, and birch. Farmers harvested these trees for lumber, fuel, and potash. Logging remained a major industry for nearly 100 years while the railroad operated in the region.
Today, logging is still important, but recreation and tourism now play a larger role. The area includes seasonal homes, outdoor recreation opportunities, and protected forest land.
Facilities and Amenities
The campground has 46 tent/RV sites and 15 lean-to sites. Eight campsites are designed for horse campers.
All restrooms include flush toilets, hot and cold running water, and token-operated hot showers. A sanitary dump station is available, but there are no hookups.
Other park features include:
A play area
Horseshoe pits
A picnic pavilion
A pond for fishing and paddling
Boat rentals
Access to miles of hiking trails
Image
Paddocks are 12' by 12' for each horse's area.
Remote sites
Osmore Pond has seven remote campsites. Four are lean-tos and three are tent sites with platforms. Remote sites 15 and 16 have 10 foot by 12 foot platforms, and site 17 has an 8 foot by 10 foot platform.
Horse camping
New Discovery State Park has an eight-site horse camping area. The group camping area includes:
Metal paddocks
A water spigot and trough for horses
A horse washing station nearby
Each campsite has a manure cart, which staff empty daily. Other pets are allowed at designated campsites.
The park offers miles of multi-use trails for hiking and horseback riding. Groton Forest is the second largest state forest in Vermont with over 26,000 acres to explore. Horseback riding routes include gravel-surfaced roads, forest highways (logging roads), the VAST trails, and the Montpelier-Wells River Rail Trail.
Horseback riders can trailer their horses to the northern parking area near the entrance to New Discovery State Park, the Kettle Pond day use parking area, or at the public boat launch at the southern end of Ricker Pond. Riders can easily access the Montpelier- Wells River Rail Trail (Cross Vermont Trail) and forest and town roads from these locations.
Picnic pavilions
Image
The pavilion at Osmore Pond seats up to 100 people
The park also has two picnic pavilions to rent. The Owl's Head Pavilion and the Osmore Pond Pavilion are both open-air log shelters with fireplaces and picnic tables. Osmore seats up to 100 people and has a restroom. Owls Head seats up to 50 and has a composting toilet nearby.
Learn more about picnic pavilions
Park Interpreter
This park has a park interpreter offering fun, hands-on activities in the new nearby Groton Nature Center. Interpreters are park staff solely dedicated to helping you learn more about the natural and cultural history of the park. Some popular activities include night hikes, nature crafts and games, campfire programs and amphibian explorations.
Check out the events calendar to see some of the programs planned during your visit.

This park is one of seven parks in Groton State Forest. All the parks are close to one another, and some are within walking distance. When you pay for entry at one park, your pass is valid at all day use parks. Together, these parks offer many recreation opportunities and natural attractions.
Welcome
Ricker Pond State Park was established in the 1930s. The park is located on the western shore of Ricker Pond and next to the Montpelier–Wells Rail Trail, which is part of the Cross Vermont Trail.
As early as 1704, Native Americans and French travelers used routes through Groton to travel between Canada and Massachusetts. Later, colonists settled this area of Vermont earlier than many other parts of the state because the waterways made travel and transportation easier.
The rocky, tree-covered hillsides were once filled with white pine, spruce, hemlock, beech, maple, and birch. Local farmers harvested these trees for lumber, fuel, and potash. Logging remained a major industry in the region for nearly 100 years while the railroad was operating.
Today, logging is still an important industry in the area. However, recreation and tourism now play a larger role. Many people visit the region for outdoor activities, and private cottages and seasonal homes are common.
Groton State Forest covers more than 26,000 acres and is the second-largest landholding managed by the Vermont Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation. The forest includes more than 17 miles of hiking trails and over 20 miles of gravel roads and multi-use trails for activities such as mountain biking and horseback riding.
Facilities and Amenities
Image
In addition to the original cottage, the Perry Merrill Cottage is also available to rent.
The campground has 26 tent/RV sites, 23 lean-tos, 5 cabins and 2 cottages. Two of the three campground restrooms include token-operated hot showers. An RV dump station is available, but there are no hookups. There is also a swimming beach, boat launch, boat rentals, and shelter for campers, as well as access to miles of hiking and biking trails.
Cottages and Cabins
Both the Original Cottage and the Perry Merrill Cottage are located on the waterfront. Each cottage sleeps four people and includes canoes for guest use.
Learn more about cottages
The five cabins are located on wooded sites. Two of the cabins have views of the water.
Cabin pricing and details
Park Interpreter
The nearby Groton Nature Center has a park interpreter who offers hands-on educational programs. Park interpreters are staff members who help visitors learn about the natural and cultural history of the park. Some popular activities include night hikes, nature crafts and games, campfire programs and amphibian explorations.

This park is one of seven parks in the Groton State Forest. These parks are all within close proximity to one another. Some are within walking distance! Entry to one provides free entry to all. Combined, the parks offer a range of activities and attractions.
Welcome
Image
Seyon Lodge is next to Noyes Pond.
One of Vermont’s best kept secrets, Seyon Lodge State Park provides rustic and welcoming facilities in the midst of the inspiring beauty of Groton State Forest. Situated on the pristine shores of Noyes Pond, the lodge provides year-round lodging and meeting facilities for individual groups, including small conferences, retreats, and gatherings.
Private rooms with shared bathrooms accommodate up to 16 overnight guests. There is a fully equipped commercial kitchen in which staff prepare meals, catering to the whims of your guests.
The Lodge at Seyon is situated within the 27,000 acres of Groton State Forest. The secluded setting allows guests to enjoy some of the most beautiful and undisturbed natural scenery in Vermont. Wildlife abounds and hiking and cross-country ski trails provide easy access to the solitude of the surrounding forests. Fly fishing for native brook trout on Noyes Pond is considered among the best in Vermont. Boat rentals for fly fishing only are available at the park. There is no swimming at Noyes Pond, but swimming is offered at the nearby Boulder Beach State Park, also located in the Groton State Forest.
Overnight Accommodations
Image
A bedroom at the lodge offers creature comforts and rustic tranquility.
Seyon Lodge offers all the best of Vermont, from the beautiful tranquility of Vermont’s state parks to the quiet, rustic charm of its B&Bs and Inns. Our comfortable accommodations teamed with the surrounding beauty of nature, our warm hospitality, great tasting healthy food, and a number of nearby attractions make for an enjoyable overnight stay.
Accommodation:
8 private, country-style rooms, each furnished with linens, towels, and quilts or blankets
shared baths
a total capacity for 16 overnight guests
a variety of possible sleeping arrangements
Free Wi-Fi connection throughout the lodge
Full-service meals upon request
a quiet and cozy common room with a fireplace
full use of the park and all it has to offer
Renting the entire lodge: Groups may rent the entire lodge up to 11 months in advance. The cost is $850 per night Monday-Thursday, and $900 Friday-Sunday. There is an additional 9% VT rooms tax. This includes sole use of the lodge’s 8 bedrooms (up to 16 people), living room with fireplace, and conference center. A delicious continental breakfast is included. One night's payment is required at the time of reservation. The balance can be paid to the park on checkout, along with meals.
Reservations: Reservations can be made by calling the park directly. Groups may reserve the entire lodge up to eleven months in advance, starting at 9 am on the first business day of the month.
Payment: Payment for 1 night is due in full at the time of reservation.
The cancellation policy: Cancel 60 days or more in advance and receive 100% refund, minus $10 cancellation fee. Cancel 59-31 days in advance and receive 50% refund. Cancel less than 30 days in advance and there will be no refund of deposit.
Dining
Image
Seyon Lodge offers farm-fresh meals made with authentic, Vermont ingredients
We strive to offer the freshest, most creative and authentic Vermont meals to our guests at Seyon Lodge, by serving Vermont's finest in-season produce, regionally raised meat and dairy. Our products are from places such as Cabot Creamery, Four Corners Farm, and the Vermont Butter & Cheese Company. With our seasonal menu, our meals give you all the warmth of a dinner at home, but add little touches of elegance for all of the style of an expensive night out.
At Seyon Lodge, we are happy to prepare breakfast and dinner for you. We will gladly accommodate most dietary needs and and we pride ourselves on creating healthy, filling, affordable meals.
Pricing ranges from $6 - $10 for breakfasts, $16 for lunches, and $20 - $25 for dinners. A Vermont meals tax of 9% will be charged in addition to meal price.
Fly fishing
Noyes Pond is perhaps the biggest draw here at Seyon Lodge, offering Vermont's sole public fly fishing-only pond. The pond offers a remote setting that anglers appreciate as much for its quiet sense of solitude as for the breeding ground it creates for native square tail brook trout. Rental row boats are available and are the only boats allowed on the pond. We have a Frequent Flyer Anglers Pass that provides unlimited fishing and boat rentals for only $125 per season.
Row boat rentals: $7.50 per hour, $25 for half day (4 to 6 hours), $40 per day (dawn to dusk), plus Vermont Sales Tax.
For more information, please either call the park at 802.584.3829 or stop by in person. Boats are offered on a first come, first serve basis. Reservations are possible by calling the park.
Meetings, Gatherings, and Conferences
Image
The conference room accommodates up to 30 people. It can be rented for meetings, crafts, showers, or conferences
Seyon Lodge State Park is a great place to hold your group's next conference, craft session, shower, or meeting. Moderately sized, accommodating up to 30 people, the conference center provides an escape from the office to set and realize goals, conduct employee training, or focus on the tasks at hand. Customize the conference facility to fit your organization’s needs from a highly professional to a more relaxed, casual setting. Free Wi-Fi (wireless internet) connection is available throughout the lodge. Lodge and conference room are universally accessible.
The friendly lodge staff can accommodate you throughout the day, providing delicious coffee and teas, fresh baked goods, and healthy, affordable lunches. Depending on the season, you may wish to take advantage of other spots within the park to hold your meeting: on the beautiful wrap-around porch, or outside near Noyes Pond. A mid-day break for fishing, a short hike, or a sit by the pond can really stir up some creativity!
Chairs and tables are provided. Mid-morning and mid-afternoon snacks are available.
Pricing: $375 per day for non-profit organizations, $500 per day otherwise.
Weddings and Ceremonies
Image
Seyon Lodge is a beautiful and idyllic spot for a country wedding
The park accommodates both outdoor services for up to 150 people and indoor ceremonies of up to 30 guests. Our friendly innkeepers are happy to discuss the various options with you.
Overnight lodging is available, and though the park is pristine and secluded, it is only 10 miles from Interstate 91 and 45 minutes from Montpelier. We offer catering options and our prices are affordable.
Pricing:
Up to 50 people = $750 site fee, and includes a 9% Vermont Rooms Tax.
50-150 people = $2,000 site fee. This provides the use of park grounds and day-use entry for guests.
Call the park at 802-584-3829 to ask questions, arrange a tour or to simply get more information.
Park Interpreter
This park has a park interpreter offering fun, hands-on activities in the new nearby Groton Nature Center. Interpreters are park staff solely dedicated to helping you learn more about the natural and cultural history of the park. Some popular activities include night hikes, nature crafts and games, campfire programs and amphibian explorations.
Check out the event calendar to see some of the programs planned during your visit.

Welcome
Image
A family hike in the notch
Welcome to Smugglers’ Notch State Park. Smugglers’ Notch is a narrow mountain pass through the Green Mountains. Tall cliffs rise nearly 1,000 feet on each side of the winding road, which closes during the winter. In earlier times, only a footpath and a trail for horses passed through the Notch.
In 1807, President Thomas Jefferson signed the Embargo Act, which stopped American trade with Great Britain and Canada. This law was difficult for many northern Vermonters because Montreal was closer than other markets in the United States. Some local residents continued trading with Canada illegally, herding cattle and carrying goods through the Notch.
Later, freedom seekers escaping slavery used the Notch as part of their journey to Canada. During Prohibition in the 1920s, smugglers again used the route to bring liquor from Canada. The road through the Notch was improved in 1922.
Facilities/Amenities
Smugglers’ Notch State Park was relocated in 2003. Historic structures built by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) were carefully moved and restored to preserve their craftsmanship. Learn more on the Vermont State Parks History page.
The new campground has sites that are more spread out, a restroom building that uses alternative energy, and easy access to Bingham Falls. The restrooms include flush toilets, hot and cold running water, and token-operated hot showers. Firewood and ice are available for sale.
Most campsites are walk-in and cannot be reached by vehicle. Because of this, and because Route 108 north of the campground is narrow, the park has very few sites that can accommodate RVs.
Day Use Area
Smugglers’ Notch State Park offers more than just the campground. Just outside the gates is a scenic corridor full of outdoor adventures.
Starting at the Barnes Camp Visitor Center, a 3.5-mile scenic highway winds through a steep mountain pass with beautiful views and many places to explore.
Visitors can walk along the wetlands boardwalk near the Barnes Camp Visitor Center or start a hike on the Long Trail. Farther up the road, the Smugglers’ Notch Picnic Area sits beside a beautiful stream.
History lovers can also see stone fireplaces built by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), a group of early conservation workers from the 1930s.
Other popular hikes include the challenging Hellbrook Trail and the well-known Sterling Pond Trail.
Activities in the notch include:
bouldering
ice climbing
cave exploring
biking
Park Interpreter
This park has a park interpreter who leads fun, hands-on activities. A park interpreter is a staff member who helps visitors learn about the park’s natural and cultural history.
Popular activities may include night hikes, nature crafts and games, campfire programs, and amphibian explorations.
Check out the events calendar to see some of the programs planned during your visit.

Welcome
Image
Underhill is within Vermont's 39,837-acre Mt. Mansfield State Forest. On the headwaters of the Brown's River, at about 2,000 feet elevation, the park lies on the west slope of 4,300 feet Mt. Mansfield, the state's highest peak. Just over the summit ridge is the Stowe ski area, one of North America's original ski resorts.
The mountain’s high elevation and harsh climate support unusual vegetation along the summit ridge. The low, stunted plants in the alpine tundra are rare in New England and resemble those found on Arctic tundra far to the north. These plants are fragile, so please stay on marked trails when hiking to the summit.
The park is best known for its hiking. Four trails lead to the summit ridge of Mt. Mansfield from Underhill State Park. Trails start just above the group camp area along the gated road from the park headquarters.
The Sunset Ridge Trail, a 3-mile route to the summit, is the most popular. Vermont’s Long Trail crosses the summit ridge, and with several trails from the other side of the mountain, hikers can create many loop options.
Trail maps and hiking information are available at the park headquarters.
Facilities and Amenities
Image
The CCC-built pavilion has a fireplace and picnic tables
The upper camp area, about 3/4 mile above the ranger station, has 7 lean-to sites and 2 tent sites. It also has pit toilets and is reserved for organized group use.
The lower camp area, near the contact station, includes 11 tent sites and 6 lean-to sites. Restrooms have cold water and flush toilets, but there are no showers.
All campsites require a short walk from the parking area. Vehicles cannot access the campsites.
The park also offers a CCC-built sheltered tent site that sleeps up to 8 people. The site includes a picnic table, a shelter fireplace (used instead of a fire ring), and 2 standing grills nearby.

Welcome
Image
Waterbury Center is a great place to picnic
Waterbury Center State Park lies on the easterly trivium of Waterbury Reservoir, a quarter mile off VT Route 100. It is an integral recreation resource in Central Vermont and one of the newer park facilities within Mount Mansfield State Forest. The Reservoir is the ninth largest body of water in the state of Vermont and was created in the 1930's by the CCC as a flood control project to protect towns and villages along the Winooski River Valley. From late spring to early fall the Reservoir is maintained to a surface area of 850 acres and has a maximum depth of 100 feet. To prepare for normal spring snow melt and runoff, the surface area is reduced to between 415 - 610 acres throughout the winter. The designed flood control capacity of Waterbury Reservoir is approximately 9,000,000,000 gallons.
Waterbury Reservoir is also a great place to fish.
Facilities/Amenities
The park is located on a 90-acre peninsula and contains:
17 picnic sites
picnic tables
charcoal grills
a swimming beach
a nature trail
trailer boat ramp
boat rentals - available until Labor Day
restrooms
a reservable meeting room
A universally accessible trail includes two accessible fishing platforms.
Boat Rentals
Boat rentals are provided through Umiak Outfitters. Prices may vary from state parks boat rental prices.
After the park closes, Umiak Outfitters will still offer boat rentals every Saturday and Sunday through Monday, October 12, 2026. They will also be offering rentals on Indigenous Peoples Day. The upper gate will stay open allowing parking in the upper lot, while the lower gate will stay closed. Park staff will be onsite and closing up the park until September 19. After that, there will be no staff present. Portable toilets will remain available, but the regular bathrooms will be closed.
Beach Access Wheelchair
A beach access wheelchair is provided to guests to use for free. Guests can call the park to make sure it will be available when they arrive, otherwise if no one is using it, it can be first come first served. There is a beach mat to provide easy access to the water.
Select parks have beach access wheelchairs. For more information on locations, check out our Beach Access Wheelchairs section on our Swimming page.
